<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases, but PRO's "moment of decision vs. moment of maximum lock-in" frame proved more durable under pressure. CON's strongest weapon was a dual-horn attack (early disclosure is either fictional estimation or forces fee-blending that kills itemization), but PRO exposed the internal tension in that attack: PRO's own opening example (a $50 ticket + $20 fee vs. a $65 all-in ticket) is precisely the comparison problem that fee-blending solves, so calling blending "concealment with a receipt" undercuts CON's own stated harm rather than PRO's case. CON's concrete late-breaking examples (card surcharges, surge pricing) were a fair answer to PRO's pressure question, but PRO's reply — that a disclosed surcharge schedule satisfies the disclosure requirement even without the exact final card chosen — blunted their force, and CON's closing request for an implicit "carve-out" reads as a concession that the core principle (disclose determinable mandatory fees before checkout) survives for the overwhelming majority of cases. CON also lost ground by having its opening clipped, dropping the small-business compliance-burden thread it opened with. PRO's answers were consistently on-format (A1/A2), sharper in exploiting contradictions, and left the cleaner decision rule for the judge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's rebuttal that CON's predicted business response (blending fees into a single sticker price) actually achieves the motion's own goal of a visible true total, directly undercutting CON's claim that early disclosure inevitably destroys transparency.</best_rebuttal>
